newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Dow dive puts question-mark over Russian rally.
newsitem.headline: Dow dive puts question-mark over Russian rally.

text.p: The shaky performance of Wall Street is sending tremors through the world's best performing emerging market and Russian investors are asking a common question -- if New York collapses, what happens to us?
"Most fund managers will see Russia as the high end of the risk curve," said Regent European Securities senior analyst Sadie Wighton.
"There is a very strong link between what America will do and what Russia will do -- obviously it is a funds flow market."
Oil producer LUKoil lost three percent by 12:30 p.m. on Monday, racking up the Dow Jones Friday loss in about one and a half hours. Most major liquid shares also declined.

Wall Street's second worst point loss ever follows rallies by both indexes this year. The Russian Trading System 21-share index is around 563 from under 200 last year and the Dow Jones is near 7,700, compared with a peak of over 8,200, from under 6,450 last year.
But Wighton like many analysts said calming forces in the Russian market may change that trend or at least muffle the effects of Wall Street worries.

Foreign investors who control the market are seeing their influence diminish day by day as hedge funds specialising in short-term moves pull out and Russians with no place else to put their money pile in.
What would happen if Wall Street had a serious correction?

"I think there would be a mark down, but I think Russian investors have provided a certain floor to Russian equity prices," Wighton said. "A lot of Western money in Russia is Russia-specific. I can't see a lot of selling in that respect."
The $100 billion capitalisation market has seen daily reported turnover highs of over $100 million but turnover can drop in half from day to day on nervousness.
Over the last month Russian banks and other investors have shown a strong influence on a shares market.

Bank funds pulled from the $50 billion, highly liquid T-bill market where yields have fallen below 20 percent from about 200 percent last year are targeting a half-dozen highly liquid shares. Other funds are seeking less liquid lower-tier shares.
Traders estimate Russian investment trading volume at from 30 percent to 70 percent but agree on the strong effect.

"Russia will continue to outperform in any scenario," said Brunswick Brokerage director Martin Diggle. "Domestic Russian buying is much less sensitive to global events than many other emerging markets.
"If Wall Street recovers, Russia will outperform, and if Wall Street collapses, Russia will go down, but by a much smaller amount than the U.S."
Some traders say the link between Moscow and New York is shorter term and more tenuous than common wisdom has it.

The Russian Trading System 21-share index of leading shares has a 0.94 correlation coefficient to the Dow Jones index since June 1996, compared to 0.97 between the Dow Jones and London's FTSE, suggesting a reasonably strong correlation.
But Russia often sees prices marked down and liquidity dry up in a falling market. "Prices are being marked down because people don't want to be hit," Diggle said.

"Currently stocks are in shorter supply than money," said one Western trader in Moscow who added that local traders overexaggerated their responses to New York based on a flawed understanding of the fundamental link between the economies.

Another said daily drops in New York of three percent or more would be reflected in opening prices the next day in Russia and that sharp drops caused fund managers to pull orders or take profits to cover positions abroad.
But longer term the link is more tenuous, and a period of Wall Street stagnation was seen as, at best, an event to highlight Russian performance.
"Russia can quite happily go up if the U.S. is flat," the trader said.
